Domestic Horse: Grays are born a darker shade, get lighter as they age, but usually keep black skin underneath their white hair coat . | Horses have excellent day and night vision, but they have two-color, or dichromatic vision; their color vision is somewhat like red-green color blindness in humans, where certain colors, especially red and related colors, appear as a shade of green.
Brown Rat: The brown rat's fur is usually brown or dark grey, while the underparts are lighter grey or brown. | One of the largest muroids, it is a brown or grey rodent with a body length of up to 28 cm long, and a tail slightly shorter than that.
Chipping Sparrow: Adults in basic plumage are less prominently marked, with a brownish cap, a dusky eyebrow, and a dark eye-line. | Adults in alternate plumage have a reddish cap, a nearly white supercilium, and a black trans-ocular line .
Great-tailed Grackle: Males are iridescent black with a purple-blue sheen on the feathers of the head and upper body, while females are brown with darker wings and tail. | Adults of both sexes have bright yellow eyes, while juveniles of both sexes have brown eyes and brown plumage like females .
Lesser Goldfinch: Females' and immatures' upperparts are more or less grayish olive-green; their underparts are yellowish, buffier in immatures. | Males are easily recognized by their bright yellow underparts and big white patches in the tail and on the wings .
Tufted Titmouse: Measurements: Length: Weight: Wingspan: A small bird, the tufted titmouse has a white front and gray upper body outlined with rust-colored flanks. | Other characteristics include its black forehead and the tufted gray crest on its head.
White-breasted Nuthatch: Coloration varies somewhat along the species' range, but the upperparts are light blue-gray, with a black crown and nape in males, while females have a dark gray crown. | Further distinctions are that the red-breasted nuthatch has a black eye line and reddish underparts, and the brown-headed and pygmy nuthatches each have a brown cap, and a white patch on the nape of the neck.
Gray Catbird: The slim bill, the eyes, and the legs and feet are also blackish.
Cedar Waxwing: Birds that have fed on berries of introduced Eurasian honeysuckles while growing tail feathers have darker orange-tipped tail feathers. | The wings are "broad and pointed, like a starling's." The tail is typically yellow or orange depending on diet.
Black Phoebe: Juveniles have browner plumage, cinnamon-brown feather tips on their body, and brown wing-bars. | The bird has brown irises and black legs, feet, and beak.
Brown-headed Cowbird: The adult male is iridescent black in color with a brown head. | The adult female is slightly smaller and is dull grey with a pale throat and very fine streaking on the underparts.
Black-capped Chickadee: It has a white belly, buff sides, and grey wings, back, and tail. | Its back is unstreaked and greenish grey, and the tail and wings are slate grey.
Common Raven: The throat feathers are elongated and pointed and the bases of the neck feathers are pale brownish-grey. | It has a longish, strongly graduated tail, at , and mostly iridescent black plumage, and a dark brown iris.
Laughing Gull: The summer adult's body is white apart from the dark grey back and wings and black head. | Its wings are much darker grey than all other gulls of similar size except the smaller Franklin's gull, and they have black tips without the white crescent shown by Franklin's.
Pied-billed Grebe: Their undertail is white and they have a short, blunt chicken-like bill that is a light grey color, which in summer is encircled by a broad black band . | They are mainly brown, with a darker crown and back.
Common Grackle: Adults have a long, dark bill, pale yellowish eyes, and a long tail; their feathers appear black with purple, green, or blue iridescence on the head, and primarily bronze sheen in the body plumage. | Adult common grackles have a long and dark bill, pale yellow eyes, and a long tail.
Barn Swallow: It has steel blue upperparts and a rufous forehead, chin and throat, which are separated from the off-white underparts by a broad dark blue breast band. | The female is similar in appearance to the male, but the tail streamers are shorter, the blue of the upperparts and breast band is less glossy, and the underparts paler.
Western Gull: It closely resembles the slaty-backed gull of Asia, but the latter species has paler eyes, a straighter bill, deeper pink legs and eye orbitals, as well as conspicuous white spots on the inner primaries when seen in flight not seen in Western Gulls. | The western gull has a white head and body, and upperparts or mantle is dark grey.
Ruby-crowned Kinglet: The bird has olive-green plumage with two white wing bars and a white eye-ring. | The kinglet has a relatively plain face and head, although the male has a scarlet-red crown patch, which is usually concealed by the surrounding feathers.
Black Vulture: It has black plumage, a featherless, grayish-black head and neck, and a short, hooked beak. | The head and neck are featherless, and the skin is dark gray and wrinkled.
Sandhill Crane: Sandhill cranes have red foreheads, white cheeks, and long, dark, pointed bills.
Ruby-throated Hummingbird: The female has a notched tail with outer feathers banded in green, black, and white and a white throat that may be plain or lightly marked with dusky streaks or stipples. | Adults are metallic green above and grayish white below, with near-black wings.
Western Bluebird: The adult male is bright blue on top and on the throat with an orange breast and sides, a brownish patch on back, and a gray belly and undertail coverts. | The adult female has a duller blue body, wings, and tail, a gray throat, a dull orange breast, and a gray belly and undertail coverts.
Plain-bellied Watersnake: Some snakes display a thin, white line between the pale belly and their darker top scales. | Some lighter-colored individuals have dark dorsal patterns.
Western Whiptail: Hatchlings are orange-yellow with dark brown-black spots or stripes. | The upper side often has light stripes, and the throat can be pinkish or somewhat orange in adults.
Little Brown Skink: Its back is typically a coppery brown color with a white or yellow underside, dark coloration running laterally from eyes to tail and like most skinks has an elongated body and short legs.
Desert Spiny Lizard: Females and juveniles have large combined dark spots on their back and belly areas, and the blue/violet and green/blue coloring is absent. | An adult male desert spiny lizard usually have conspicuous blue/violet patches on the belly and throat, and a green/blue color on their tails and sides.
Ornate Tree Lizard: Monomorphic males will maintain this orange throat coloration for life, however, polymorphic males will either retain their orange throat color or they will develop a yellow throat color as they mature. | The blue patch can be described as a characteristic that heavily contributes to sexual selection since females tend to mate with males that have larger blue spots.
Pickerel Frog: Small pickerel tadpoles are yellowish to yellowish brown in color; as they grow their color changes to an olive green, which eventually changes to gray brown on top and cream colored underneath. | == Distinguishing features == The pickerel frog is a large gray or tan frog marked with seven to twenty-one irregular rectangular dark brown spots which are oriented in two columns down its back.
Gray Treefrog: A unique aspect of the appearance of the gray treefrog is that its legs feature a dark band-like pattern which then contrast sharply with the black-marked bright yellow or orange under the sides of its legs and arms. | Young frogs will also sometimes maintain a light green color, only turning gray or darker green once adulthood is reached.
Southern Leopard Frog: It is green or brown in color with a yellowish ridge along each side of the back. | Rounded dark spots occur on the back and sides; a light spot is seen on each tympanum.
Southern Toad: The color of the head, back and sides varies from brick red to mottled grey, brown and black while the underparts are pale, sometimes with dark spots on the chest.
Western Toad: It has a white or cream dorsal stripe, and is dusky gray or greenish dorsally with skin glands concentrated within the dark blotches. | Large young have prominent dorsal and ventral spotting and yellow feet.
Dusky Smooth-hound: This shark is an olive grey or brown in color, and may have shades of yellow or grayish white. | Newborns have lighter gray edges on their fins and have tail fins edged in white.
Big Brown Bat: Its dorsal fur is reddish brown and glossy in appearance; its ventral fur is lighter brown. | Unlike in other species more affected by white-nose syndrome, big brown bats are able to retain more of their body fat throughout hibernation.
Thirteen-lined Ground Squirrel: It is brownish, with 13 alternating brown and whitish longitudinal lines on its back and sides, creating rows of whitish spots within dark lines. | == Description == It is brownish, with 13 alternating brown and whitish longitudinal lines on its back and sides, creating rows of whitish spots within dark lines.
Swamp Rabbit: The head and back are typically dark or rusty brown or black, while the throat, ventral surface, and tail are white, and there is a cinnamon-colored ring around the eye. | Additionally, the back portions of the swamp rabbit's hind legs are orange, in contrast to the tan or white feet of the eastern cottontail.
Uinta Ground Squirrel: Their fur is brown to cinnamon in color, being paler on the underside and grey on the sides of the head and neck. | The tail is buff with a grey underside, as distinct from the ochraceous or reddish color found in closely related species such as Belding's or Wyoming ground squirrels.
Eastern Mole: The eastern mole has grey-brown fur with silver-grey underparts, a pointed nose and a short tail. | == Description == The eastern mole has grey-brown fur with silver-grey underparts, a pointed nose and a short tail.
Southern Flying Squirrel: == Description and ecology == Southern flying squirrels have grey-brown fur on top with darker flanks and are a cream colored underneath. | They have large dark eyes and flattened tails.
Tree Swallow: The bill is black, the eyes dark brown, and the legs and feet pale brown. | The tree swallow has glossy blue-green upperparts, with the exception of the blackish wings and tail, and white underparts.
Savannah Sparrow: The Savannah sparrow has a typically sparrow-like dark-streaked brown back, and whitish underparts with brown or blackish breast and flank streaking. | The flight feathers are blackish-brown with light brown or white border.
Little Blue Heron: Their eyes are yellow and their legs are greenish. | The legs and feet become black.
Spotted Towhee: Adult males have a generally darker head, upper body and tail with a white belly, rufous sides, white spots on their back and white wing bars. | It has a round body with bright red eyes and dull pink legs.
Common Yellowthroat: Adult males have black face masks which stretch from the sides of the neck across the eyes and forehead, which are bordered above with white or gray. | Common yellowthroats are small songbirds that have olive backs, wings and tails, yellow throats and chests, and white bellies.
California Towhee: The California towhee's coloring is dull brown overall with light rust undertail covert feathers and buff or rust-colored streaks at the throat. | The California towhee's color pattern is matte brown all around, barring a rusty patch beneath its tail and around its bill.
American Herring Gull: First-winter birds are gray-brown with a dark tail, a brown rump with dark bars, dark outer primaries and pale inner primaries, dark eyes, and a dark bill, which usually develops a paler base through the winter. | Adults are white with gray back and wings, black wingtips with white spots, and pink legs.
Acorn Woodpecker: The adult acorn woodpecker has a brownish-black head, back, wings and tail, white forehead, throat, belly and rump. | The white neck, throat, and forehead patches are distinctive identifiers.
Ring-necked Duck: The adult female has a grayish brown angular head and body with a dark brown back, a dark bill with a more subtle light band than the male, grayish-blue feet and brown eyes with white rings surrounding them. | It has two white rings surrounding its gray bill, a shiny black angular head, black back, white line on the wings, a white breast and yellow eyes.
Gadwall: It can be distinguished from that species by the dark orange-edged bill, smaller size, the white speculum, and white belly. | The female is light brown, with plumage much like a female mallard.
Muscovy Duck: A blackish or dark red knob can be seen at the bill base, which is similar in colour to the bare skin of the face. | The plumage is predominantly black, with large white patches on the wing; the back and wing feathers being iridescent and glossy in males, while the females are more drab.
Sanderling: The winter bird is very pale, almost white apart from a dark shoulder patch. | Later in the summer, the face and throat become brick-red.
Black-necked Stilt: Downy young are light olive brown with lengthwise rows of black speckles on the upperparts – essentially where adults are black – and dull white elsewhere, with some dark barring on the flanks. | Such individuals often have some white or grey on top of the head and a white or grey collar separating the black of the hindneck from that of the upper back.
Common Merganser: Adult males in breeding plumage are easily distinguished, the body white with a variable salmon-pink tinge, the head black with an iridescent green sheen, the rump and tail grey, and the wings largely white on the inner half, black on the outer half. | Females and males in "eclipse" are largely grey, with a reddish-brown head, white chin, and white secondary feathers on the wing.
Eastern Kingbird: Adults are grey-black on the upperparts with light underparts; they have a long black tail with a white end and long, pointed wings. | The bird is predominantly dark gray with white underbelly and pointed wings.
White-winged Dove: They have a blue eye ring, and their legs and feet are brighter pink/red. | Adults have a ring of blue, featherless skin around each eye and a long, dark mark on the lower face.
Common Gallinule: == Description and ecology == The gallinule has dark plumage apart from the white undertail, yellow legs and a red frontal shield.
Florida Softshell Turtle: Stripes in the same color are also found on the face and neck. | Hatchlings have a lighter carapace with yellow and orange markings and a carapacial rim.
Green Sea Turtle: The common name refers to the usually green fat found beneath its carapace, due to its diet strictly being seagrass, not to the color of its carapace, which is olive to black. | mydas limbs are dark-colored and lined with yellow, and are usually marked with a large dark brown spot in the center of each appendage.
California Slender Salamander: Typically, the dorsal coloration is black, with a stripe that is reddish or brown. | The ventral marking is dark with minute whitish dots.
Cope's Gray Tree Frog: Both species vary in color from mottled gray to gray-green, resembling the bark of trees. | Both species are variable in color, mottled gray to gray-green, resembling the bark of trees.
Cuban Tree Frog: Cuban tree frogs are mostly gray, brown, or green, with young frogs having more green coloration than adults.
Northern Leopard Frog: It varies from green to brown in dorsal color, with large, dark, circular spots on its back, sides, and legs. | Also, a pale stripe runs from the nostril, under the eye and tympanum, terminating at the shoulder.
Squirrel Tree Frog: Males may also possess a relatively large, conspicuous lateral body stripe, with thicker stripes being more attractive to female frogs. | There are several color variations, but most commonly they are green and look very much like the American green tree frog.
Horn Shark: A small species typically measuring 1 m in length, the horn shark can be recognized by a short, blunt head with ridges over its eyes, two high dorsal fins with large spines, and a brown or gray coloration with many small dark spots. | The dorsal coloration consists of various shades of gray or brown with many small dark spots, though these may be absent in older sharks; the underside is yellowish.
Nurse Shark: Nurse sharks are also subject to piebaldism, a genetic condition that results in a partial lack of body pigmentation and a speckled body.
Eastern Red Bat: The eastern red bat has distinctive fur, with males being brick or rusty red, and females being a slightly more frosted shade of red. | Both male and female eastern red bats have distinctive shoulder patches of white fur.
Townsend's Chipmunk: In much of its range, it is the only chipmunk; it can be identified by its tail which is grayish above and reddish below, and by its brown coloration with indistinct tawny stripes.
Mountain Cottontail: It has pale brown fur on the back, black-tipped ears, a white-grey tail, and a white underside. | It is a medium- to small-sized rabbit with pale brown fur, white undersides, a two-colored tail, and black-tipped, rounded ears with densely furred insides.
House Mouse: In the wild they vary in color from grey and light brown to black , but domesticated fancy mice and laboratory mice are produced in many colors ranging from white through champagne to pink. | They have short hair and some, but not all, sub-species have a light belly.
Least Chipmunk: The back is marked with five dark brown to black stripes separated by four white or cream-colored stripes, all of which run from the nape of the neck to the base of the tail. | The body is gray to reddish-brown on the sides, and grayish white on the underparts.
Hermit Thrush: The underparts are white with dark spots on the breast and grey or brownish flanks. | They have pink legs and a white eye ring.
Steller's Jay: This dark coloring gives way from the shoulders and lower breast to silvery blue. | The primaries and tail are a rich blue with darker barring.
Northern Harrier: The male's plumage is darker grey than that of the hen harrier, and the female is also darker and more rufous.
Eurasian Collared-Dove: The tail feathers are grey-buff above, and dark grey and tipped white below; the outer tail feathers are also tipped whitish above. | It is grey-buff to pinkish-grey, slightly darker above than below, and with a blue-grey underwing patch.
Ruddy Duck: In summer, it has a rich chestnut body with a bright blue bill. | The female and first-year male are brownish, somewhat like the winter male but with a blurry stripe across the pale cheek patch.
Greater Yellowlegs: The body is grey-brown on top and white underneath; the neck and breast are streaked with dark brown. | The greater yellowlegs and the greenshank share a coarse, dark, and fairly crisp breast pattern as well as much black on the shoulders and back in breeding plumage.
Spotted Sandpiper: The body is brown on top and white underneath with black spots. | Adults have short yellowish legs and an orange bill with a dark tip.
Least Sandpiper: This species has yellow-green legs and a short, thin, dark bill. | They have a light line above the eye and a dark crown.
Tricolored Heron: Adults have a blue-grey head, neck, back, and upper wings, with a white line along the neck. | Its legs and feet turn from dark yellow in nonbreeding birds to pink in breeding adults.
Palm Warbler: It has brownish-olive upper parts and thoroughly yellow underparts with bold rufous breast and flank streaking.
Indigo Bunting: In the adult female, the beak is light brown tinged with blue, and in the adult male the upper half is brownish-black while the lower is light blue. | In fall and winter plumage, the male has brown edges to the blue body and head feathers, which overlap to make the bird appear mostly brown.
Blue-winged Teal: The adult male has a greyish blue head with a white facial crescent, a light brown body with a white patch near the rear and a black tail. | Both sexes have sky-blue wing coverts, a green speculum, and yellow legs.
Brown Thrasher: The western brown thrasher is distinguished by a more cinnamon upper part, whiter wing bars, and darker breast spots than T.rufum rufum. | However, the wood thrush has dark rounded spots on its under parts rather than the brown thrashers' elongated streaks, has dark eyes, shorter tail, a shorter, straighter bill , and is a smaller bird.
Yellow-bellied Sapsucker: The juvenile is a dark olive-brown colour overall, with a buff-striped head and a streaked crown. | Sometimes, this is the only place on the head a female will have red colouration, if it has any at all, as the female rarely has a black head with a few buff spots.
Hairy Woodpecker: Adults are mainly black on the upper parts and wings, with a white or pale back and white spotting on the wings; the throat and belly vary from white to sooty brown, depending on subspecies. | Adult males have a red patch or two side-by-side patches on the back of the head; juvenile males have red or rarely orange-red on the crown.
Orange-crowned Warbler: The orange-crowned warbler has olive-grey upperparts, yellowish underparts with faint streaking and a thin pointed bill. | sordida – resident in south California and northwest Mexico == Description == The orange-crowned warbler has olive-grey upperparts, yellowish underparts with faint streaking and a thin pointed bill.
Common Loon: Breeding adults have a plumage that includes a broad black head and neck with a greenish, purplish, or bluish sheen, blackish or blackish-grey upperparts, and pure white underparts except some black on the undertail coverts and vent. | It has a dark grey to black head, neck, and upperparts, with white throat, cheeks, and underparts.
Eastern Towhee: Adults have rufous sides, a white belly, and a long, dark tail with white edges. | Males have a black head, upper body, and tail; these parts are brown in the female.
California Quail: Adult males are gray and brown colored, with a black face outlined by white stripes. | Females are a plainer brown color and do not have the facial stripes.
Diamondback Terrapin: The carapace coloring can vary from brown to grey, with a lighter plastron , and its body color can be grey, brown, yellow, or white. | Carapace more narrow and elongated than in other subspecies, brown to blackish and with rounded bumps along the entire ridge; head and forelegs with few to no black spots.
California King Snake: A wide range of color morphs exist in the wild; they are usually found with alternating dark and light bands ranging in color from black and white to brown and cream. | California kingsnakes stripes and bands are essential to their survival as the patterns camouflage the snakes body to hide from predators.
Six-lined Racerunner: The six-lined racerunner is typically dark green, brown, or black in color, with six yellow or green-yellow stripes that extend down the body from head to tail. | Between the stripes are dark-colored fields ranging from dark brown to black and pale-colored fields near ventral scales on each side.
Woodhouse's Toad: The dorsal surface of this toad is grayish-brown or yellowish-brown and it is speckled with small dark spots.
Northern Two-lined Salamander: This salamander is yellow or yellowish-brown, with two black stripes running down the back which tends to break up after the base of the tail. | The flanks are mottled grayish or brown.
Northern Slimy Salamander: The northern slimy salamander is typically an overall black in color, with numerous silvery spots or gold spots across its back. | == Description == The northern slimy salamander is typically an overall black in color, with numerous silvery spots or gold spots across its back.
Northern Cricket Frog: Many have a brown or orange stripe down the center of their back and a triangular marking on the top of their head. | These frogs are majorly in grey, green, and brown color with blotching patterns.
Round-tailed Ground Squirrel: They have no fur markings, instead having a uniform sandy color, which matches the soil they burrow in.
Orca: The tail fluke is also white on the underside, while the eyes have white oval-shaped patches behind and above them, and a grey or white "saddle patch" exists behind the dorsal fin and across the back. | Variations such as nicks, scratches, and tears on the dorsal fin and the pattern of white or grey in the saddle patch are unique.
Grey Seal: Males tend to have a light pattern on a dark background, while females tend to have the opposite — a dark pattern on a light background, often with a noticeably light belly. | Compared to the harbour seal, the grey seal has a longer, more sloped snout, a flatter head, and eyes which are set farther apart.
Northern House Wren: All subspecies show a faint eye-ring and eyebrow and have a long, thin bill with a blackish upper mandible, and a black-tipped yellowish or pale grey lower mandible.
Boat-tailed Grackle: Adult males have entirely iridescent black plumage, a long dark bill, a pale yellowish or brown iris, and a long keel-shaped tail. | She is also distinguished by her shorter tail and tawny-brown coloration, which covers the body apart from the darker wings and tail.
Greater Roadrunner: A crest of brown feathers sticks up on the head, and a bare patch of orange and blue skin lies behind each eye; the blue is replaced by white in adult males , and the orange is often hidden by feathers. | The neck and upper breast are white or pale brown with dark brown streaks, and the belly is white.
Black-bellied Whistling-Duck: It has a long pink bill, long head and longish legs, pale gray head and mostly gray-brown plumage. | The belly and tail are black, and the body plumage, back of the neck and cap are a rich chestnut brown.
Bewick's Wren: Its plumage is brown on top and light grey underneath, with a white stripe above each eye. | At about 14 cm long, it is grey-brown above, white below, with a long white eyebrow.
Loggerhead Shrike: Measurement ranges Length: Weight: Wingspan: The adult plumage of the loggerhead shrike is grey above with a white to pale grey breast and black tarsi and feet. | The loggerhead shrike can be distinguished from the northern shrike by its smaller size, darker grey plumage, and larger black face mask that covers the eye completely.
Rose-breasted Grosbeak: The adult female has dark grey-brown upperparts – darker on wings and tail – a white supercilium, a buff stripe along the top of the head, and black-streaked white underparts, which except in the center of the belly have a buff tinge. | The adult male in breeding plumage has a black head, wings, back, and tail, and a bright rose-red patch on its breast; the wings have two white patches and rose-red linings.
Common Goldeneye: Adult males have a dark head with a greenish gloss and a circular white patch below the eye, a dark back and a white neck and belly. | Their legs and feet are orange-yellow.
Lesser Scaup: The adult males in definitive basic plumage have a black, iridescent head and a small tuft at the hindcrown, a black breast, a whitish-grey back, wings with darker vermiculations and black outer and greyish-brown inner primary remiges. | Both sexes have white secondary remiges, a blue-grey bill with a smallblack "nail" at the tip and grey feet; the drakes have a bright yellow iris, while that of females is orange to yellow varying with age and that of immatures is brown.
Northern Pintail: Its upperparts and sides are grey, but elongated grey feathers with black central stripes are draped across the back from the shoulder area. | The adult female is mainly scalloped and mottled in light brown with a more uniform grey-brown head, and its pointed tail is shorter than that of the male; it is still easily identified by its shape, long neck, and long grey bill.
Golden-crowned Sparrow: Other than a plain gray nape, the adult's upperparts are grayish-brown, with broad brownish-black streaks on the back and scapulars, and an unstreaked rump. | In the breeding season, the golden-crowned sparrow has a broad yellow central crown stripe which becomes pale gray towards the back of the head.
Western Kingbird: Although the western is often misidentified as Cassin's kingbird, Couch's kingbird, or the tropical kingbird due to the yellow coloration, it can be distinguished from these other species through its black, squared tail with white edges. | Adults are a combination of both gray and yellow plumage, along with crimson feathers that are hidden until courtship or against intruders.
Black-and-white Warbler: Both sexes have black and white crowns with a white eyebrow, black streaking on a white belly, black wings with two white wing bars, a black tail, a black-and-white streaked back, streaky undertail coverts, and grey-black legs and feet. | Breeding males have a black-and-white streaked throat and black cheek, while females have a grey cheek and a white-cream coloured throat and sides.
Red-headed Woodpecker: Adults are distinctly tricolored, with a black back and tail, a white belly and rump, and a red head and neck. | The wings are black with white secondary flight feathers.
Red-breasted Merganser: The male has a dark head with a green sheen, a white neck with a rusty breast, a black back, and white underparts. | Males have a bottle green head with a double crest and females have a rusty head with a white fore neck and chin.
American Redstart: Their breast sides are also orange, with the rest of their underparts white. | The breeding males are unmistakable, jet black above apart from large orange-red patches on their wings and tails.
Pine Warbler: These birds have white bellies, two white wing bars, dark legs and thin, relatively long pointed bills; they have yellowish 'spectacles' around their eyes. | Adult males have olive upperparts and bright yellow throats and breasts; females and immatures display upperparts which are olive-brown.
Summer Tanager: Adult males are rose red and similar in appearance to the hepatic tanager, although the latter has a dark bill; females are orangish on the underparts and olive on top, with olive-brown wings and tail.
Royal Tern: The royal tern has a stout orange-red bill, pale silvery-gray upperparts, and white underparts. | Juvenile royal terns are similar to non-breeding adults, differing in the juveniles having darker gray to blackish marks on the wings, and a yellower bill.
Red-breasted Nuthatch: The adult has blue-grey upperparts with cinnamon underparts, a white throat and face with a black stripe through the eyes, a straight grey bill and a black crown. | Its back and uppertail are bluish, and its underparts are rust-coloured.
Painted Bunting: Its colors, dark blue head, green back, red rump, and underparts, make it extremely easy to identify, but it can still be difficult to spot since it often skulks in foliage even when it is singing.
Broad-headed Skink: Juveniles are black and with 5 white or yellowish stripes and a blue tail. | Females have five light stripes running down the back and the tail, similar to the Five-lined Skink.
Texas Horned Lizard: They also have dark lines that span from the eyes to the tip of the horns and a characteristic solid white line with a few black circular splotches on either side. | Coloration varies depending on the environment in order to blend in with the color of the ground, ranging from a yellow or reddish-brown for deserts to a tannish brown for prairies.
Tropical House Gecko: Normally coloured in black and brown bands, this gecko can slowly change its colour based on its ambient temperature and lighting; its scales vary in colour from dark brown to light grey.
Gold Dust Day Gecko: There are three rust-coloured transverse bars on the snout and head; the upper part of the skin around the eye is blue. | The body colour is a bright green or yellowish green or rarely blue.
Greater Short-horned Lizard: The color is gray, yellowish, or reddish-brown, and there are two rows of large dark spots on the back.
Eastern Hognose Snake: The belly tends to be a solid gray, yellow, or cream-colored. | In this species, the underside of the tail is lighter than the belly.
Eastern Narrow-mouthed Toad: The colors on its sides are generally faded, but its dorsum is dark and broad with various light or dark spots, mottling, or patches that cover the light strip along its middorsal area. | They vary in color from brown and grey to green, often with black and white spotting.
Red-spotted Toad: It has a flattened head and body, and a light grey, olive or reddish brown dorsum with reddish or orange skin glands.
